title: Vera skoro! Zurich to Berlin, the Fast Short Life of the Abstract Dance
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Zürich, the Child of the Emigrants

stops.name: Zurich, birth of Vera Lämmel
stops.campa: On the 28th of May a daughter is born in Zurich to Rudolf Lämmel, a Viennese doctor of physics who will spend his life reforming schools, and to Sonja Axelrod, daughter of Pavel Axelrod, ideologue of the Mensheviks, comrade of Plekhanov, kefir-maker of the Russian exile. Two revolutions meet in the cradle: the new pedagogy and the old conspiracy. The child is named Vera: faith. She will keep the faith, but it will be a faith in pure movement, and she will spend it all in twenty-five years.
suggested_refs: Portrait photographs of Vera Skoronel in the Nachlass, Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln (Bestand 066)

stops.name: Zurich, the naming: Vera, skoro!
stops.campa: In the flat of the Lämmels the small girl never walks; she runs, spins, arrives everywhere before she is called. A Russian relative of her mother's, watching her flash through the rooms, laughs and cries out 'Vera, skoro!': Vera, quickly! The household takes it up, and the child takes it further: she welds the adverb to herself and makes of it a name, Skoronel. In this register a name is a fate spoken early. Quickly: the whole life is in it, the speed of the dances, and the soon of the end.
suggested_refs: The stage name Skoronel itself, from the Russian skoro, 'quickly', the childhood anecdote preserved in the German Wikipedia and the Tanzarchiv biography

stops.name: Zurich: the Semmler-Rinke school, rhythmic gymnastics
stops.campa: At six years old the running child is given a discipline for her speed. From 1912 she attends the courses in rhythmische Gymnastik at the Semmler-Rinke school in Zurich, where little bodies are taught to carry the beat in the limbs after the new doctrine of the age. The reform-pedagogue father approves: the body too is a school. Vera learns to count with her arms before she can write an essay, and the counting never leaves her; years later her technique will still be built on the drilled, repeated, circling form.
suggested_refs: The rhythmic-gymnastics movement of the 1910s, Dalcroze method schools of Switzerland

stops.name: Zurich: death of the mother, Sonja Axelrod
stops.campa: In the year the world turns, the mother dies. Sonja Axelrod-Lämmel is thirty-five; Vera is ten. In the same months the grandfather Pavel Axelrod leaves the Swiss exile for Petrograd, where the revolution he argued for half a century has arrived without asking him how. The Russian half of the household goes silent in two directions at once: into the grave and into history. The girl keeps the Russian word in her name and the orphan's velocity in her body, and is raised henceforth in her father's world of schools.
suggested_refs: Pavel Axelrod, Menshevik ideologue, the Zurich exile circle of the Emancipation of Labour group

stops.name: Zurich, the Laban school of Suzanne Perrottet and Käthe Wulff
stops.campa: At Easter 1919 the twelve-year-old enters the Laban school of Zurich, kept by Suzanne Perrottet and Käthe Wulff, women of the master's first circle, veterans of the holy mountain at Ascona. Here the child of gymnastics is given the larger gospel: movement as a language older than music, the swing and the scale of Laban's new writing of the body. The school still breathes Monte Verità air; Dada is shouting a few streets away at the Cabaret Voltaire, and Perrottet has danced in it. Vera begins her true schooling in the middle of the whirlwind.
suggested_refs: Suzanne Perrottet's Zurich Laban school, photographs in the Kunsthaus Zürich Perrottet archive

stops.name: Zurich, the meeting with Rudolf von Laban
stops.campa: At thirteen she stands before Laban himself, the magus of the movement choirs, and studies under his eye. The canon of the dance keeps this meeting as an anointing: the man who has mapped the swinging scales of human effort looks at the small fast Swiss girl who cannot hold still, and the lineage passes. She will quarrel with his heirs in print one day, measuring him coolly against Wigman, but the first laying-on of hands is his, in Zurich, before her fourteenth year.
suggested_refs: Karl Toepfer, Empire of Ecstasy, Skoronel studied with Laban at age thirteen

stops.name: Loheland, three months among the women of the Rhön
stops.campa: In 1921 she goes north into Germany for the first time, three months at the Loheland school in the Rhön hills near Fulda, the settlement of women who build their own houses, weave their own cloth, breed dogs, photograph light, and hold gymnastics to be a way of life rather than an exercise. The fifteen-year-old lives inside a working utopia of the body. Loheland gives her what Zurich could not: the sight of women running an entire world by discipline of movement. She will build such a house herself before she is twenty-two.
suggested_refs: The Loheland settlement at Künzell in the Rhön, its photographic archive of gymnastic bodies

stops.name: Dresden: entry into the Wigman school, Bautzner Straße
stops.campa: In 1922 the sixteen-year-old comes to Dresden, to the school Mary Wigman has opened on the Bautzner Straße two years before, and is counted among the first pupils of the house. The Hexentanz woman, high priestess of the absolute dance, takes the fast Swiss girl into the daily rite: bare feet on the studio floor, the gong, the drum, improvisation driven until the body confesses. Vera arrives a Laban child and is remade a Wigman one, though the geometry sleeping in her will one day out-abstract them both.
suggested_refs: The Mary Wigman school, Bautzner Straße 107, Dresden, now the Villa Wigman

stops.name: Dresden, the fellowship of the first pupils
stops.campa: The studio on the Bautzner Straße in these years is a forge of the whole coming age. Beside Vera work Gret Palucca, Yvonne Georgi, Hanya Holm, Aenne Grünert; Leni Riefenstahl passes through the classes; and here she meets Berthe Trümpy, the Swiss patrician who co-founded and finances the school, eleven years her elder, the friend of her fate. Every axis of the German dance to come crosses this floor. In the canon of the movement this room is what Athens is to philosophy: everyone was young there together.
suggested_refs: Group photograph of Wigman with Skoronel, Palucca, Georgi, Trümpy, Kreutzberg and others (Bildindex der Kunst & Architektur, obj 32025256)

stops.name: Dresden, dancing in Wigman's first group
stops.campa: Wigman forms her first dance group from the best of the school, and Vera dances in it, the corps of the new art in its first campaigns, the evenings that carry the absolute dance out of the studio and onto the stages of Saxony and the Reich. Seventeen years old, she learns what a group is: not a frame for a soloist but a single instrument of many bodies. The lesson lodges deep. No dancer of the era, the chroniclers will write, pursued the group work more fiercely than she.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the first Wigman-Tanzgruppe, 1923-24, Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln

stops.name: Dresden: the leave-taking, diploma of the first generation
stops.campa: By the summer of 1924 the training is complete: Vera Skoronel, eighteen, stands among the first finished dancers the Wigman school has made. The teacher's mark is on her: the seriousness, the darkness, the belief that dance is knowledge, but the pupil is already turning against ecstasy itself, toward the drilled figure, the repeated mechanical form, the square. An offer comes from the industrial west: a theater of her own kind to build. She takes the fast train out of the Wigman heaven into the coal smoke.
suggested_refs: The Wigman school diploma generation of 1924, school records, Mary Wigman Archive, Akademie der Künste Berlin

segments.name: The Ruhr and Darmstadt, the First Troupe of Her Own

stops.name: Oberhausen, dance direction of the Vereinigte Städtische Bühnen
stops.campa: At eighteen she is handed a theater. The united municipal stages of Oberhausen, Hamborn and Gladbeck give her the dance direction, and she builds there one of the first modern dance groups at any German theater, a troupe standing free of opera and operetta, serving nothing but the new dance. A girl one year out of school commands rehearsal in the black country of chimneys and slag, drilling miners' daughters in abstract form. In the canon of the art this is the founding wonder: the youngest ballet mistress in the Reich.
suggested_refs: The Theater Oberhausen, house of the Vereinigte Städtische Bühnen Oberhausen-Hamborn-Gladbeck

stops.name: Oberhausen: Das böse Quadrat, the Evil Square
stops.campa: With her Ruhr troupe she makes Das böse Quadrat, the Evil Square, a dance-play in which geometry itself is the demon. Bodies are pressed into the figure of the square and the square is wicked: repetition, right angles, the machine-form set loose among the living. The piece scandalizes and triumphs from 1924 onward and follows her for years, the first banner of what she will name abstract dance. In an age dancing its feelings, an eighteen-year-old sets a shape on stage and lets the shape do the willing.
suggested_refs: Skoronel's ghostly colored-pencil choreographic drawings, shown in Die absoluten Tänzerinnen, Georg-Kolbe-Museum Berlin, 2021

stops.name: Hamborn, the second stage of the union
stops.campa: The troupe plays the circuit of the union: Hamborn, the mining city on the Rhine plain, its theater full of men with coal still under their fingernails and their families in Sunday cloth. Here the abstract dance is set before an audience that has never been told what dance must be, and therefore does not know to be offended. Skoronel counts these evenings among the proofs: the new form does not need the initiated. The body drilled to pure rhythm speaks to people who live by shift-whistles better than swans ever did.
suggested_refs: The municipal theater culture of the 1920s Ruhr, Vereinigte Städtische Bühnen playbills

stops.name: Gladbeck, the third stage, and the reckoning
stops.campa: At Gladbeck the third of the united stages receives her group, and the ledger receives its verdict. The Ruhr in 1925 is a land squeezed between occupation, inflation's scar and the pit-head; the municipal purse cannot carry an autonomous dance troupe, however famous its Evil Square. The engagement that made her a prodigy dissolves under her for money, not for art: the first lesson in the economics of the new dance, which she will spend the rest of her life outrunning. The troupe scatters; the choreographer packs her drawings.
suggested_refs: Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln biography, the Ruhr engagement ended by financial collapse

stops.name: Darmstadt, ballet mistress at the Hessisches Landestheater
stops.campa: For the season of 1925-26 she goes south to Darmstadt as dance director of the Hessian state theater, a court house with columns, the opposite pole to the coal towns. Nineteen years old, she sets modern group work inside a repertory machine built for opera ballets, and learns how an institution resists a form. Darmstadt is brief and instructive: the theater will not be the vessel. What the abstract dance needs is its own house, its own school, its own bodies raised from the first exercise. Berlin is the answer forming.
suggested_refs: The Hessisches Landestheater Darmstadt on the Karolinenplatz, now the Haus der Geschichte

segments.name: Berlin, the Trümpy-Skoronel School and the Congresses

stops.name: Berlin-Wilmersdorf, co-direction of the Trümpy school
stops.campa: In 1926 she comes to Berlin and the fate closes its circuit: Berthe Trümpy, her elder from the Dresden studio, who has kept a school of her own in the capital since 1924, takes her as colleague and co-director. The house becomes the Schule Trümpy-Skoronel. The pact is exact: Trümpy gives money, order, administration; Skoronel gives the burning method. The celebrated soloist and the patrician organizer, two Swiss women in Wilmersdorf, set out to build the most modern dance school in Germany, and by every account they do.
suggested_refs: Lotte Jacobi's photographs of the Skoronel-Trümpy dance group, c. 1930

stops.name: Berlin, the lesson of May 1926: the arms set free
stops.campa: An observer sits in her class in May 1926 and records a heresy: Skoronel trains the arms as an independent instrument, separate from the movement of the trunk, driving clear counter-rhythms through a single body: one pulse in the feet, another cutting across it in the hands. The chroniclers will say she is teaching, thirty years early, the polycentric isolations that jazz dance will one day claim for itself. In her studio it is simply the abstract method: the body not as a soul's gesture but as an orchestra of parts.
suggested_refs: The May 1926 teaching observation preserved in the Skoronel literature (German Wikipedia, after the Tanzarchiv documents)

stops.name: Magdeburg, the first German Dancers' Congress: the breakthrough
stops.campa: In June 1927 the whole warring church of the German dance assembles at Magdeburg for the first Tänzerkongress: Laban's party, Wigman's party, the theater ballets, the critics. Into this synod steps Skoronel, twenty-one, and her solos carry the hall; the chronicle records it as her decisive breakthrough. With her group she gives Der gespaltene Mensch, the Split Man, Bruno Schönlank's speech-chorus made flesh, proletarian voices and abstract bodies in one machine. She leaves Magdeburg a name of the first rank, the youngest power at the council.
suggested_refs: The Stadthalle Magdeburg, built for the 1927 Deutsche Theaterausstellung that housed the first Tänzerkongress

stops.name: Berlin, the Volksbühne: Der gespaltene Mensch and Erweckung der Massen
stops.campa: On the 21st of February 1928, at the Volksbühne on the Bülowplatz, the Split Man is given again in the Magdeburg casting, and beside it rises a new work of hers: Erweckung der Massen, the Awakening of the Masses. In the people's own theater the abstract dance and the workers' speech-chorus are joined: the drilled group as an image of the class waking into a single body. The canon keeps the pairing as her political sacrament: geometry placed at the service of the awakening multitude, form itself made comrade.
suggested_refs: Bruno Schönlank's Sprechchor movement and the Volksbühne am Bülowplatz (today Rosa-Luxemburg-Platz)

stops.name: Berlin-Wilmersdorf, the new house: Blüthgenstraße 5
stops.campa: The school receives its temple. The architect Alfred Gellhorn raises for Trümpy and Skoronel a building of their own in Wilmersdorf at Blüthgenstraße 5 by the Westfälische Straße, dwelling and dance-hall in one, built 1927 and enlarged 1928, praised as the most modern house of its kind: a school constructed around the new body as deliberately as a laboratory around its instrument. Loheland's lesson is fulfilled: women building the house of their own discipline. The war will later erase the building; the canon keeps its address.
suggested_refs: Alfred Gellhorn's Tanzschule Trümpy building, Blüthgenstraße 5, Berlin-Wilmersdorf (1927/28, destroyed)

stops.name: Essen, the second Dancers' Congress, the woman in white
stops.campa: June 1928, Essen: the second Tänzerkongress, the great family portrait of the German dance. In the famous group photograph Skoronel stands luminous in an elegant white dress among the assembled masters, twenty-two and already a chapter of the history. To Essen too belongs her Trilogisches Tanzspiel, the three-part dance-play made with the composer Rosenberg and the designer Heinz Porep, which has its debut in this city: her largest architecture of the abstract group form, dance freed of story and of music's illustration alike, movement composed from movement.
suggested_refs: The Essen 1928 Tänzerkongress group photograph, Skoronel in the white dress

stops.name: Berlin, Der moderne Tanz: the father prints the daughter's doctrine
stops.campa: Rudolf Lämmel publishes Der moderne Tanz, and at the book's heart stands his daughter: her treatise Der abstrakte Tanz fills its pages with eleven plates, and the libretto of the Tanzspiel is printed whole. The reform-pedagogue who once wrote to explain relativity now writes that she is the most significant dance-poet the Wigman school has produced. Father and daughter close the circle begun in the Zurich nursery: the theory of the fast body, set down in type. It is the fullest scripture of her doctrine that survives.
stops.quote: In the 'Quadrat' the abstract feeling was still conveyed in movement forms determined by the anatomical nature of the human body, so the new dance gives the dissolution of these forms into their dynamic linear components and the projection of movement curves into the plane of planimetric force elements.
stops.quote_source: Libretto of the Tanzspiel, printed in Rudolf Lämmel, Der moderne Tanz (Berlin, 1928); English rendering after Karl Toepfer, Empire of Ecstasy (1997)
suggested_refs: Rudolf Lämmel, Der moderne Tanz (1928), with Skoronel's chapter 'Der abstrakte Tanz', pp. 144-170

stops.name: Berlin, the essay on Laban
stops.campa: In 1929 she publishes her essay on Laban, the pupil of thirteen now weighing the magus in print. Skoronel writes as she choreographs: exactly, structurally, without incense. The dance, she argues in these years, must become an objective, transmittable art governed by strict formal law: composition, not confession. Between rehearsals at the Blüthgenstraße she is building the theory of the abstract dance essay by essay, the only dancer of her generation whom the chroniclers call a dance-poet and a systematician in the same sentence.
suggested_refs: Skoronel's theoretical manuscripts, 'Über abstrakten Tanz', Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln (Bestand 066)

stops.name: Berlin, solo evening at the Bachsaal
stops.campa: On an autumn evening she dances at the Bachsaal on the Lützowstraße, the concert hall of the Klindworth-Scharwenka conservatory, one of the consecrated rooms of the Berlin solo dance. The celebrated soloist of the congresses gives the capital her cycle of abstract dances: arms circling in machine-time, the thrust, the strike, the turn, the monotonous form repeated until it opens. The critics have learned her category by now and write it as she taught them to: not expression-dance but abstrakter Tanz, a thing with laws, danced by its lawgiver.
suggested_refs: Der Tanz, Fachzeitschrift für deutsche Tanzkultur, the Berlin dance press of 1929

stops.name: Berlin, the two essays on Wigman
stops.campa: In 1930 she publishes her double portrait of the teacher: Mary Wigmans Führertum and Mary Wigmans Kompositionsstil, Wigman's leadership, Wigman's style of composition. The first pupil measures the founder with a compass, honoring the priestess by analyzing the rite. It is the abstract dancer's homage: not adoration but anatomy, the ecstatic school described in the cool grammar of form. The Dresden gods are given their exact due by the one heretic they raised themselves, and the essays enter the permanent scripture of the movement.
suggested_refs: Skoronel's essays 'Mary Wigmans Führertum' and 'Mary Wigmans Kompositionsstil' (1930)

stops.name: Munich, the third Dancers' Congress, with her students
stops.campa: June 1930: the third and last of the great congresses, at Munich. Skoronel comes now not only as the famous soloist but as a head of school, her students around her, the abstract method embodied in a generation she has trained from the first exercise. The congress quarrels, as congresses do, over theater and freedom, Laban and Wigman, bread and art; she stands in it as the proof that a doctrine can be taught. It is her last synod. The movement has four more summers; she has not quite two.
suggested_refs: Programme of the 3. Deutscher Tänzerkongress, München 1930

stops.name: Berlin-Wilmersdorf, the students: Charlotte Bara comes to the school
stops.campa: Through the halls of the Blüthgenstraße pass the bodies that will carry her out into the century: Hanna Berger, Ilse Meudtner, Lisa Czóbel who will dance in the premiere of The Green Table, Oda Schottmüller who will die under the executioner as a resister, and from the south comes Charlotte Bara, the Gothic dancer of Ascona, who takes her training with Trümpy and Skoronel in Berlin and bears the method back to the Teatro San Materno above the lake, where the holy mountain of Laban's youth keeps its own theater.
suggested_refs: Charlotte Bara's Teatro San Materno, Ascona, the pupil's temple above Lago Maggiore

stops.name: Berlin, the Dante inscribed: alles, alles Gute
stops.campa: On the first of February 1931 she takes a volume of Dante's Divine Comedy in Stefan George's translation, the sternest German ever made of the poem of the other world, and writes a farewell in it for a departing student of the school, wishing her everything, everything good, and signs and dates the page. The book survives her; the dealers keep it under glass. In this register the relic reads itself: the dying dancer's hand, Dante's journey through the dark, and a blessing given twice over.
stops.quote: Ich wünsche Ihnen alles, alles Gute. Vera Skoronel, 1. Feb. 1931
stops.quote_source: Autograph dedication in Dante, Göttliche Komödie, trans. Stefan George, copy from the Trümpy-Schule, Berlin (antiquarian record, Librairie du Cardinal)
suggested_refs: The signed Trümpy-Schule copy of Stefan George's Dante with Skoronel's dedication of 1 February 1931

stops.name: Berlin-Wilmersdorf, the sickness in the blood
stops.campa: The blood itself turns against the fastest body in Berlin. Through 1931 the sickness the chronicles call a Blutkrankheit wears her down; those near her speak of chronic exhaustion, of a woman enchanting and madly gifted who disturbs every communal peace and cannot spare herself, who teaches and composes against the failing of her own instrument. The name given in the nursery keeps its second edge now: skoro, quickly, soon. She does not stop working. The abstract dance was always a discipline against the body's nature; she holds the discipline.
suggested_refs: Contemporary recollections of Skoronel preserved in the Trümpy and Skoronel papers, Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln

stops.name: Berlin, death of Vera Skoronel
stops.campa: On the 24th of March 1932, in Berlin, Vera Skoronel dies of the disease of the blood. She is twenty-five years old. The Weimar dance loses its severest architect ten months before the Republic itself begins to die; she is spared the sight of the movement she helped build being marched into step by the coming state. The canon closes her ledger cleanly: one Evil Square, one Split Man, one Awakening of the Masses, one Tanzspiel, one doctrine of the abstract dance, one school full of students. Twenty-five years.
suggested_refs: Obituaries in the Berlin dance press, March 1932 (Der Tanz)

stops.name: Berlin, Fritz Cremer casts the right hand
stops.campa: At the deathbed the young sculptor Fritz Cremer takes plaster and casts her right hand: the hand that drew the ghostly colored-pencil figures, that wrote the doctrine of the abstract dance, that cut counter-rhythms through the air of the Blüthgenstraße studio. The gesture belongs to the old rite of the death mask, but what is kept of the dancer is not the face: it is the instrument. The cast survives as her one bodily relic: the fastest hand in the German dance, stopped and made permanent at twenty-five.
suggested_refs: Fritz Cremer's plaster cast of Vera Skoronel's right hand, taken on her deathbed, 1932

stops.name: Berlin, burial in the Friedhof Wilmersdorf
stops.campa: They bury her in the cemetery of Wilmersdorf, the borough of her school, a short walk from the house Gellhorn built for the abstract dance. Trümpy, the friend and other half of the pact, survives her by fifty-one years and carries the school on alone before merging it away; the grave stays in the quarter where the work was done. The dancers of Berlin lay the fastest of their number into the slowest of all figures, the ground, and the name on the stone is the childhood cry: quickly.
suggested_refs: The grave of Vera Skoronel, Friedhof Wilmersdorf, Berlin

stops.name: Berlin, the name dances again: Tanztheater Skoronel
stops.campa: Fifty-two years after the burial, in West Berlin, the choreographer Judith Kuckart founds a free dance-theater company and gives it the dead girl's name: Tanztheater Skoronel. The papers meanwhile gather in Cologne, at the German Dance Archive, brought by the brother Boris and out of Trümpy's estate: the drawings, the manuscripts on the abstract dance, the photographs by Lotte Jacobi. The canon's verdict stands as Toepfer writes it: no dancer of the Weimar era pursued the modernist group form more fiercely. The name keeps its promise: Vera, quickly, again.
suggested_refs: Vera Skoronel Nachlass, Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln (Bestand 066); Judith Kuckart, Eine Tanzwut: Das TanzTheater Skoronel
